asked: FDA reviewed our petition and won't exempt our new pigment from certification. What does that mean for the listing and for using batches that aren't certified?
answer:
FDA will not exempt your new pigment from certification, which means that any color additive mixture containing this pigment must be certified if intended for use in foods, drugs, cosmetics, or coloring the human body. Batches of the pigment that are not certified according to the requirements in §80.35(a) and (b) are not permitted for use.

21 CFR 70.3(j) [4] defines "straight color" as a color additive listed in parts 73, 74, and 81 of this chapter, and includes lakes and such substances as are permitted by the specifications for such color.  

21 CFR 80.35(a) [1] requires that any color additive mixture containing one or more straight colors listed in part 74, together with any diluents listed in such subparts for use with such straight colors, shall be certified if intended for use in foods, drugs, or cosmetics, or in coloring the human body.  

21 CFR 80.35(b) [2] provides that a color additive mixture prepared from a previously certified batch of one or more straight colors, with or without any diluent that has been listed in part 73 of this chapter for use in mixtures, shall be exempt from batch certification if the straight color used has not changed in composition in any manner whatsoever since its certification and if it is simply mixed with the approved diluents for exempt mixtures.  

21 CFR 80.35(c) [3] requires that a person requesting additions to the list of diluents authorized for the purposes described in paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section shall submit a petition in accordance with the provisions of §71.1 of this chapter, each such petition being accompanied by the fee prescribed in §70.19 of this chapter, unless there is an advance deposit to be used for prepayment of such fees. The exemption under (b) depends on no change in composition of the straight color since its certification and mixing only with approved diluents; otherwise, certification is required.

The responsible person must submit this information within 30 days of receiving the written request [4]. This request does not require public disclosure; any information submitted in response to such a request may be withheld under section 552(b)(3) of title 5, and adverse event reports—including new medical information—shall not be publicly disclosed unless personally identifiable information is redacted [5]. The identity of the fragrance ingredients must be provided if requested by the FDA, and the submission must occur within 30 days after receipt of the request [4].

The requirement to submit a list of specific fragrance ingredients in response to an FDA request is required under FD&C Act § 605(f) [4].  

A serious adverse event report, including new medical information related to it, may not be publicly disclosed unless all personally identifiable information has been redacted, as such reports are considered records about an individual under the Privacy Act and protected from public release [5].

No provision requires the identity of specific fragrance ingredients to be made public; such information is protected under section 552(b)(3) of title 5 and shall not be disclosed unless personally identifiable information is redacted [5].

The time frame for submitting a response to an FDA fragrance ingredient request is 30 days after receipt of the written request [4].  

The submission of information in response to an FDA request under § 605(f) may be withheld from public disclosure under section 552(b)(3) of title 5, and such reports are protected as records about individuals under the Privacy Act [5].

FDA may suspend a facility's registration if it determines that conditions or conduct associated with the facility are material to food safety and pose a risk of public health harm, such as during an active investigation of a foodborne illness outbreak directly linked to the facility or when FDA finds it necessary to protect public health based on such conditions [1]. The grounds for suspension include circumstances where FDA determines that a foodborne illness outbreak is likely or already occurring due to conditions at the facility [2], and when FDA concludes that actions by the facility are material to food safety [3].

FDA must notify the owner, operator, or agent in charge of the facility, in writing, of circumstances that may lead to withdrawal of the exemption, and provide an opportunity for the owner, operator, or agent to respond in writing within 15 calendar days of receipt of the notification [6]. FDA must also consider the actions taken by the facility to address the circumstances that may lead to withdrawal of the exemption [7].

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to answer whether there is a specific time limit beyond 15 calendar days for responding, or what additional procedural safeguards exist during the suspension process.

answer:
Yes, registration and product listing provisions apply to your facility because it manufactures or processes cosmetic products for distribution in the United States [1].  

Registration applies if a person owns or operates a facility that engages in manufacturing or processing of a cosmetic product for distribution in the United States, and such activity occurs on or after December 29, 2022 [1].  

Product listing applies to each cosmetic product manufactured or processed at the facility; for products marketed on or after December 29, 2022, the responsible person shall submit a cosmetic product listing not later than one year after December 29, 2022, or within 120 days of first marketing if the product is first marketed after that date [3]. Updates to the listing are required annually if there has been no change in product details [3].  

A single registration covers all cosmetic products manufactured or processed at a facility, regardless of the number of responsible persons involved [1]. The registration must include: the facility's name, physical address, email address, and telephone number; for any foreign facility, the contact for the United States agent and, if available, electronic contact information; the facility registration number (if assigned); all brand names under which cosmetic products are sold; and the product category or categories and responsible person for each cosmetic product manufactured at the facility [2].  

A single listing submission may include multiple cosmetic products with identical formulations or differing only in color, fragrance, or flavor [3]. Each listing must include: the facility registration number(s); the name and contact of the responsible person; the name of the cosmetic product as it appears on the label; the applicable cosmetic category or categories; a list of ingredients including fragrances, flavors, or colors identified by common or usual names; and a product listing number assigned by the Secretary [3].  

Registration must be renewed biennially with the Secretary [1]. An abbreviated renewal process is available if no updates have been submitted to the registration since the most recent submission [1].  

These provisions do not address Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) requirements.

asked: We're a distributor whose name is on the label; the product is made by a contract manufacturer. A user was hospitalized after using our hair-straightening cream. Who reports, by when, and what goes in the report?
answer:
A distributor whose name is on the label and who distributes a cosmetic product made by a contract manufacturer is considered the "responsible person" under FD&C Act § 605(a) and must report any serious adverse event associated with the use of the product in the United States. The responsible person must submit a serious adverse event report accompanied by a copy of the label on or within the retail packaging no later than 15 business days after receiving the report [2]. If new and material medical information related to the serious adverse event is received within one year of the initial report, it must be submitted to the Secretary no later than 15 business days after such information is received [2]. The distributor must receive reports through contact information provided on the label, including a domestic address, telephone number, or electronic contact information [3]. Records related to each adverse event report must be maintained for six years; if the responsible person qualifies as a small business under section 364h and does not engage in manufacturing of the product described in subsection 364h(b), records may be kept for three years [4].

The requirement to submit a serious adverse event report within 15 business days after receiving it applies regardless of whether the distributor is the manufacturer or merely the distributor, as long as the name appears on the label and the product is distributed by the responsible person [2]. The report must include a copy of the label on or within the retail packaging [2].

The responsible person (distributor) shall submit to the Secretary a serious adverse event report accompanied by a copy of the label on or within the retail packaging no later than 15 business days after the report is received by the responsible person [2].  
A new and material medical information related to a serious adverse event must be submitted no later than 15 business days after such information is received, provided it is received within one year of the initial report [2].  
The distributor shall receive reports through contact information included on the label, including domestic address, telephone number, or electronic contact information [3].  
Records related to adverse event reports must be maintained for a period of 6 years; if the responsible person qualifies as a small business under section 364h and does not engage in manufacturing of the product described in subsection 364h(b), records may be maintained for 3 years [4].

A batch of eye shadow rejected for microbial contamination may be considered adulterated under FD&C Act § 601(c), which provides that a cosmetic is adulterated if it has been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become contaminated with filth or rendered injurious to health. The presence of microbial contamination that results from improper processing or storage could satisfy this condition, making the batch adulterated under § 601(c). However, the FD&C Act does not explicitly permit reprocessing of an adulterated cosmetic; therefore, reworking the batch is not authorized by statute and would likely violate the law. The absence of a provision allowing reprocessing for microbial contamination means that FDA regulations do not govern or authorize such rework under current statutory language.

FD&C Act § 601(c) [21 U.S.C. 361(c)] governs the condition under which a cosmetic is deemed adulterated due to insanitary conditions resulting in potential contamination with filth or rendering injurious to health. No FDA rule governs the reprocessing of a batch rejected for microbial contamination because the available statutory provisions do not authorize, permit, or specify any procedure for reworking an adulterated cosmetic. The statute does not contain a provision permitting reprocessing under any condition, and therefore, no specific regulatory authority authorizes such action [1].  

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to answer whether rework is permitted beyond the definition of adulteration in § 601(c). While microbial contamination may trigger adulteration under that section, there is no provision permitting or requiring reprocessing. asked: FDA believes our lash adhesive likely caused serious injuries. If we refuse to stop distribution, what can FDA do, and what records can it see about the affected lots?
answer:
If FDA believes that the lash adhesive likely caused serious injuries, and if the company refuses to stop distribution, FDA can initiate a regulatory hearing under 21 CFR 814.47(b)(1) to determine whether to issue an order temporarily suspending approval of the PMA. If FDA determines there is a reasonable probability that continued distribution would cause serious, adverse health consequences or death, it may proceed with such a hearing as provided in 21 CFR 814.47(b)(1). FDA can also, under 21 CFR 814.47(b)(2), conduct the hearing pursuant to part 16 of this chapter and may waive, suspend, or modify any part 16 procedure if immediate action is necessary to protect public health. If the PMA holder fails to request a hearing within the timeframe specified by FDA in the notice of opportunity for hearing, FDA shall deem that failure to be a waiver under 21 CFR 814.47(b)(3). In such cases, FDA may issue an order temporarily suspending approval of the PMA if it determines there is a reasonable probability that continued distribution would cause serious adverse health consequences or death, as specified in 21 CFR 814.47(c). These provisions do not specify what records FDA can see about affected lots; therefore, the available sources do not provide information on which specific records FDA may access regarding the affected lots.

21 CFR 814.47(a)(2) authorizes FDA to issue an order temporarily suspending approval of a PMA if it determines there is a reasonable probability that continued distribution would cause serious, adverse health consequences or death.  
21 CFR 814.47(b)(1) requires FDA to initiate and conduct a regulatory hearing if it believes there is a reasonable probability that the continued distribution of a device under an approved PMA would cause serious, adverse health consequences or death.  
21 CFR 814.47(b)(2) provides that any such regulatory hearing shall be conducted by FDA pursuant to part 16 of this chapter and may include waiver, suspension, or modification of procedures if immediate action is necessary to protect public health.  
21 CFR 814.47(b)(3) states that FDA shall deem the PMA holder's failure to request a hearing within the timeframe specified by FDA to be a waiver.  
21 CFR 814.47(c) authorizes FDA to issue an order temporarily suspending approval of the PMA if either the holder does not request a hearing or, after consideration of the administrative record, FDA determines there is a reasonable probability that continued distribution would cause serious adverse health consequences or death.  
21 CFR 814.47(d) requires FDA to proceed expeditiously but within 60 days to hold a hearing on whether to permanently withdraw approval of the PMA after issuing a temporary suspension order.  

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to specify what records FDA can see about the affected lots.
